p1.a: Yes, I do, especially history *museums*. I find it fascinating to see real objects that people used hundreds of years ago. Whenever I travel, I try to visit at least one, even if I only have a couple of hours.

p1.q: Is traditional art popular in your country?
p1.a: Fairly popular, yes. Things like calligraphy and pottery are still appreciated, and you can find beautiful *folk* crafts in the old markets. However, I'd say younger people are more interested in modern digital art these days.

Very much. I mostly read *novels*, both in Arabic and in English, because they help me relax and also improve my vocabulary. Recently I've also started reading some classical *poetry*, which is challenging but rewarding.

p2.cue: Describe a historical place you have visited.
points: and explain why you found it interesting
p2.a: I'd like to describe the old town of Al-Balad in Jeddah, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. I went there about two years ago with my cousins during the winter holiday, when the weather was pleasant enough to walk around all afternoon. What struck me first was the *architecture*. Many of the houses are several storeys high and are built from coral stone, with beautiful carved wooden balconies and window screens. We also explored a small *museum* inside one of the restored houses, where we saw old *costumes*, coffee pots and other everyday *artefacts*. I found the place interesting because it showed me how people lived before air conditioning and modern cities. The narrow lanes stay surprisingly cool, which shows how clever traditional builders were. More importantly, the visit made me proud of our *heritage* and made me realise how important it is to protect places like this for future generations.

p3.q: Why is it important to protect historical buildings?
p3.a: I think they are an important part of a nation's *cultural identity*. They show us where we come from and how our ancestors lived. They also bring economic benefits, because tourists travel long distances to see *ancient* places. Once a historic building is destroyed, it can never truly be replaced, so protecting it is really an investment in the future.

p3.q: Do you think globalisation is a threat to traditional cultures?
p3.a: To some extent, yes. Global brands, films and social media spread the same lifestyle everywhere, so local *traditions* can start to seem old-fashioned to young people. On the other hand, the internet also allows small communities to share their crafts, food and *festivals* with the whole world, so I'd say it is both a threat and an opportunity.

writing.q: Some people think that governments should spend money on preserving old buildings and traditional arts, while others believe this money should be spent on modern needs such as housing and transport. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
essay: Governments everywhere face difficult choices about how to spend limited public funds. While some people argue that preserving *historical sites* and traditional arts should be a priority, others feel that money is better spent on practical needs like housing and transport. In my view, both are important, but a modest, well-planned investment in *heritage* is fully justified.

Those who favour spending on modern needs have a strong case. In rapidly growing cities, many families cannot afford decent homes, and congested roads waste millions of hours each year. For these citizens, a restored palace or a new *exhibition* may seem like a luxury when basic services are lacking. Supporters of this view also point out that *contemporary* infrastructure directly improves people's quality of life and boosts economic productivity.

On the other hand, there are convincing reasons to protect the past. *Ancient* buildings, *monuments* and traditional crafts are central to a nation's *cultural identity*, and once they are lost they cannot be rebuilt. Moreover, heritage can be an economic asset rather than a burden. Cities such as Istanbul and Cairo attract millions of tourists every year largely because of their *architecture* and history, creating jobs in hotels, restaurants and local workshops. Funding for traditional *craftsmanship* also keeps alive skills that might otherwise disappear within a generation.

In conclusion, although housing and transport must remain the main priorities for public spending, I believe a reasonable share of the budget should be used to preserve historical buildings and traditional arts, since they enrich society both culturally and financially.
